passages.title: Sociohistorical Interpretations of Art
passages.text:
Most sociohistorical interpretations of art view a body of work as the production of a class, generally a dominant or governing class, imposing its ideals. For example, Richard Taruskin writes in his *Oxford History of Western Music* that one of the defining characteristics of “high art” is that “it is produced by and for political and social elites.” What Taruskin and others fail to clarify, however, is that there are two different ways that art, historically, was “produced by and for political and social elites.”

The first way was for a member of the elite to engage a well-known artist to produce something for display. For instance, if one commissions a famous architect to design one’s house, that may reflect great credit on one’s taste, even if one finds the house impossible to live in. The second way was to create, or to have created, a work that expressed and mirrored one’s ideals and way of life, like Raphael’s frescoes in the Vatican apartments commissioned by Pope Julius II.

Sociohistorical critics like Taruskin prefer to deal with art produced the second way, because it enables them to construct a subtle analysis of the way such art embodied the ideology of the elite, whatever the identity of the artist. For this kind of analysis to work, however, it must be the case that the elite had a recognizable identity and displayed some kind of consensus about the world and the way life was to be lived, and it must also be the case that we can eliminate the possibility that artists subverted the ideals of the patron for their own reasons.

Historically, the two social classes able to commission art were the aristocratic, or governing class, and the well-to-do middle class, what used to be called the bourgeoisie. The taste of the aristocracy and the upper middle class has not always been apt to produce an art that endures. In his characterization of nineteenth-century English culture, cultural critic Matthew Arnold identified the aristocracy as Barbarians, interested largely in fox hunting and gaming, and the middle class as Philistines, obsessed with respectability. As a result, the more talented artists sometimes had to find a place in the margins of the establishment—engaged by a rich patron with eccentric tastes, for example.

Moreover, a great deal of art that went against the grain of elite values was paid for by the establishment unwillingly and with misgivings. Because some of this art endured, the sociohistorical critic, like Taruskin, must engage in an analogue of Freudian analysis, and claim that in hidden ways such art embodied the ideals of the elite, who were unaware that those ideals are revealed by work of which they overtly disapproved.

summaries.standard:
****Central Topic / Purpose****

The relationship between art and the elites / *to clarify a misconception*

****Main Point****

While Taruskin and other sociohistorical interpreters of art think that the relationship between art and elites is one in which artists expressed the ideals of the elites for whom they were making art, there are reasons to think that in many cases this relationship doesn't hold.

****Passage Map****

P1 - Introduces the mainstream view (art = representation of elites' ideals) and offers thesis that there's more to the story.

P2 - Presents the "two ways" - 1. You hired an artist because they're trendy/famous and so it'll help your reputation. 2. You hired an artist to create something that embodies your ideals.

P3 - Clarification that the 2nd way is what the mainstream uses, and then possible problems with the second way.

P4 - Explains that mainstream elite taste did not always support enduring art, so talented artists sometimes depended on eccentric patrons rather than a representative elite consensus.

P5 - Bringing up cases where the artists specifically disobeyed the wishes of the elite, and showing how the 2nd way analysis would be particularly ill-conceived here.

****Other Commentary****

The first sentence has a huge foreshadowing clue as to the purpose / main point of the passage, since it starts with "most X's have done Y". That almost always leads into an author's pivot (but, yet, however, recently), just as it does in the end of the first paragraph.

Paragraph 4 challenges an easy inference from surviving art to a unified elite ideology: elite taste could be hostile to enduring work, and support could come from patrons with eccentric tastes. This does not mean elites literally had no ideals.

The "Freudian analysis" line in the final paragraph is also very tricky. The author is saying, "take a situation where we know that Artist X was hired by Elite Y. Y asked X to make art expressing certain ideals, but X flouted those wishes and made something that X wanted to make, which is something that Y doesn't like. If Taruskin is looking at this art and saying, *this art reflects A's ideals*, then he must be assuming that Y's ideals are not consciously known to Y, otherwise why would Y have requested something very different from Y got?"

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipating Answer
explanationBlocks.body: We want to hear something like, "these sociohistorical folks are silly for thinking that we can look at art and say *this represents the ideals of the elite*, when there are definitely complicating factors that might make that incorrect."

choices.text: Historically, art was primarily commissioned by the governing classes and the well-to-do middle classes, despite the fact that this arrangement was not apt to produce art that endures.
choices.explanation:
It should scare us that the language in this answer comes primarily from the 4th paragraph, which is just a body paragraph. Main point language is almost always in the 1st or Last paragraph.

This answer is missing the essential piece of the passage, the relationship between art and ****the ideals**** of the elite. If our author was leaving us with one sentence by which to remember this passage, it wouldn't be "Art was primarily paid for by rich people", as this answer does.

choices.text: Sociohistorical interpretations of art that claim that art merely reflects the ideals and values of the elite classes are overly simplistic.
choices.explanation: The author identifies two patronage relationships, then explains that an ideological reading requires a recognizable elite consensus and no subversion by artists. Eccentric patrons and reluctantly funded work complicate that picture. The conclusion is that treating art as a straightforward reflection of elite ideals is too simple, not that elites have no ideals.

choices.text: Historically, patrons of the arts have generally been more interested in what being a patron would do for their reputation than in influencing the development of the arts.
choices.explanation:
Our author wants to acknowledge that in some cases patrons are more concerned about their reputation, in other cases they're more concerned about having their ideals expressed.

But our author never quantifies or compares the relative frequency of those two situations. We can't find any language in the passage saying, "If you add it all up, there are more cases of reputation-art than ideals-art."

The idea of *influencing the development of art* is pretty far adrift from *expressing the elites' ideals*, so this answer also gets out of scope.

choices.text: Sociohistorical critics must engage in a form of Freudian analysis to justify, in light of apparently conflicting evidence, the claim that works of art embody the ideals of the elite.
choices.explanation: The Freudian comparison addresses the final complication: art funded despite elite disapproval. It does not capture the earlier distinction between commissioning art for display and commissioning art to express ideals, or the problem of eccentric rather than representative patrons. It is too narrow for the whole passage.

choices.text: There have historically been two distinct ways in which members of the elite classes have had art produced for them.
choices.explanation:
Yes, the author said this, and yes it's part of our author correcting the misconception (since Taruskin and others tend to only focus on one way).

But this misses the headline discussion which is about whether or not we can use art to infer things about the ideals of the elites who commissioned the art.

This is just a subsidiary idea; it's a premise that allows the author to say, "and *this* is why it's not always clear that art expresses the elites' ideals".

questions.prompt: In using the phrase "something for display" (first sentence of the second paragraph), the author most probably means art that

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body: The first two sentences of the second paragraph provide this line and an example of it.

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipating Answer
explanationBlocks.body:
The example we're given sounds like "for display" has less to do with the ordinary meaning of "hanging on my wall", and more to do with "displaying to my friends how cool I am that I had Picasso design my bathroom sink".

So the answer should capture something like "to seem cool, by being associated with a trendy artist."

choices.text: allowed the patron to make a political statement to the world
choices.explanation: Nothing in those two sentences makes it sound like the artist was chosen *as a political statement*.

choices.text: could be used to attract customers to the patron’s business
choices.explanation: The only example we got was *used to make people think their house is cool*. We have no support for the idea that artists were commissioned to get people to come to a store.

choices.text: was meant to create an impression that reflected positively on the patron
choices.explanation: Cool, by association. That's what we were looking for. This matches up well with the example, in which a rich person pays a famous architect to design their house, so that it may *reflect great credit on their taste*.

choices.text: was representative of the artist’s broader body of work at the time
choices.tag: Out of Scope: representative of the artist's work
choices.explanation:
Nothing in those sentences makes it sound like rich people specifically wanted representative pieces of art. They just wanted the well-known name attached, from what we've read.

That sink is a *Picasso*, whether or not it's representative of Picasso's broader body of work or just a new direction he was tinkering with.

choices.text: provided the patron with personal satisfaction
choices.explanation: Although we can probably infer that *indirectly* patron derived personal satisfaction, it wasn't from the art itself, but rather from how impressed their rich friends would be that Picasso designed the bathroom sink.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that the attitude of Matthew Arnold toward the aristocratic and middle classes can best be described as one of

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text / Anticipating Answer
explanationBlocks.body:
If we look at the lead-in sentence to Matthew Arnold (the 2nd sentence of the 4th paragraph), it helps us know the function of the Matthew Arnold quote. The lead-in is saying "the taste of the aristocracy and upper middle class *has not always been apt to produce an art that endures*".

Daaaaaamn! In scholarly language, that was a sick burn. Our author be sayin' that their taste in art was strugglin'.

What does Arnold say?
aristocracy: Barbarians
upper middle class: Philistines who were obsessed with respectability.

The vocab in that sentence is tough. Barbarians are "uncultured, savage". Philistines is a term that means "the unsophisticated masses".

So we want something that sounds like Arnold's attitude was "disparaging / unimpressed".

choices.text: respect
choices.explanation: He called them barbarians and philistines, both of which are insults.

choices.text: empathy
choices.explanation: There's no sense in which Arnold is saying, "ya know, I can relate to them".

choices.text: indifference
choices.explanation: He didn't use neutral adjectives, as one who is indifferent might. He used two insulting terms.

choices.text: disappointment
choices.explanation:
This is pretty close. It is negative, like (E). And (E) is very strongly negative, so we might feel like this is safer.

The problem is that "disappointment" sort of presupposes that you had high hopes and ended up crestfallen. It's an attitude parents use about their kids or teachers use about their students.

It's harder to support the idea that Arnold had high hopes for these elites but then came to find out that they were actually lacking in artistic prowess.

choices.text: scorn
choices.explanation: Although this sounds like it might be too strong, calling someone "a *barbarian"* or saying that someone is "*obsessed* with respectability" is a scornful insult.

questions.prompt: The passage raises all of the following as complications for the sociohistorical interpretation of art EXCEPT:

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipating Answer
explanationBlocks.body: The complications include artists subverting patrons' ideals, patrons with eccentric tastes, elite taste that did not foster enduring art, and works funded despite elite disapproval. Identify which offered case is absent from those discussions.

choices.text: artists who subverted the ideals of patrons for reasons of their own
choices.explanation: This is what is talked about at the end of the 3rd paragraph and the beginning of the 5th.

choices.text: patrons who had eccentric tastes not reflective of the ideals of the elite classes
choices.explanation: The last sentence of the 4th paragraph is saying, "Since the mainstream elite had barbaric 'ideals', the talented artists who produced the enduring art we're now analyzing reflected eccentric elites, not mainstream."

choices.text: patrons whose taste was unlikely to produce art that endured
choices.explanation: The second sentence of paragraph 4 says aristocratic and upper-middle-class taste was not always apt to produce enduring art. The following sentences illustrate the problem and explain why talented artists sometimes needed eccentric patrons.

choices.text: patrons who bought artwork solely for the purpose of reselling that artwork for a profit
choices.explanation: We never heard about elites who *bought* art *solely* for ****re-sale.****

choices.text: patrons who unwillingly bought artwork that conflicted with their values
choices.explanation: The first sentence of the 5th paragraph discusses this.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that Taruskin's position commits him to which one of the following views?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body:
The closest language to "T's position *commits him* to" is found in the 5th paragraph, where it says that *T* *****must***** *engage in an analysis in which he's claiming that even though the rich people explicitly disapproved of this art created by their disobeying artist, the art still somehow reflected their ideals*.

The other part could be the middle of the 3rd paragraph, in which we hear necessary language like "For this kind of analysis to work, it *must be the case that* ".

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipating Answer
explanationBlocks.body:
He's committed to thinking that "sometimes we outwardly dislike something that aligns with our ideals"?

or, if it's testing the 3rd paragraph, he's committed to thinking that "the elite had recognizable ideals / the artists didn't subvert those ideals".

choices.text: The most talented artists throughout history have been those whose work embodied the ideology of the elite in hidden ways.
choices.explanation: The passage never singles out "the most talented" artists. In the 4th it says that "the more talented" ones would have probably been commissioned by eccentric elites.

choices.text: The most successful artists working today are those whose work reflects the ideology of the elite.
choices.tag: Too Strong: the most successful artists / Out of Scope: working today
choices.explanation: Taruskin (and the passage) never makes any claims about artists working today. And we never talk about *the most successful* ones.

choices.text: If it endures, high art that appears to undermine the ideology of the elite actually supports that ideology in some way.
choices.explanation: This is coming from the last sentence of the passage. Since some art that endured was made by artists who went against elite values (and yet Taruskin holds that art reflects the elites' values), Taruskin is committed to thinking that art that goes against a set of values could somehow reflect / support those values.

choices.text: Typically, art that reflects the ideology of the elite is produced by artists who are themselves members of the aristocratic or middle classes.
choices.explanation:
We can't find any generalization that says that "more than 50% of the time", if art reflected the elite, then the artist was rich or middle class.

Taruskin's supposition is that typically art reflects the elite, and he never discriminates based on the background of the artists themselves.

choices.text: The most talented artists throughout history have been those whose work subverted the ideology of the elite in subtle ways.
choices.tag: Too Strong: the most talented in history
choices.explanation: The passage mentions more talented artists sometimes finding eccentric patrons, but does not identify the most talented artists throughout history as those who subverted elite ideology. More and most are comparative expressions here, not fixed percentages such as a top half or top tenth.

questions.prompt: The primary function of the third paragraph is to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipating Answer
explanationBlocks.body:
The third paragraph is where the author remind us that T & Co. like to use the second way, but this second way has two dubious assumptions:
- the elite actually had consistent ideals to express
- the artists expressed those ideals, rather than subverting them and doing whatever they felt like

So maybe something like, "Describe the assumptions undergirding the type of analysis that T & Co. like to do"

choices.text: reject a possible response to the argument made in the first paragraph
choices.tag: Out of Scope: reject a response
choices.explanation:
There isn't really an "argument" in the first paragraph. If we said that T & Co's position in the first paragraph was an "argument", then this paragraph would be setting up possible reasons to reject that argument, not *rejecting* *****a response***** *to the argument.*

If we said that the author's position in the first paragraph was an "argument", then this paragraph would be elaborating on her position, not rejecting a possible response to it.

choices.text: identify assumptions relied upon by a type of analysis referred to in the first paragraph
choices.explanation:
The type of analysis referred to in the first paragraph is T & Co's habit of thinking "From this art, we can revere-engineer the ideals of the elite who paid for it".

In the 3rd paragraph, our author is saying "for this analysis to work, it must be the case that X was true and it must also be the case that Y was true".

It's fair to call those necessary requirements "presuppositions / assumptions / underlying givens".

choices.text: present an argument that weakens the argument made in the second paragraph
choices.explanation: The argument made in the second paragraph is that there are two ways in which art was produced for elites. The third paragraph does nothing to weaken that idea.

choices.text: offer additional evidence for the conclusion reached in the second paragraph
choices.tag: Bad Match: conclusion reached in 2nd paragraph
choices.explanation:
There isn't any conclusion in the second paragraph; it just outlined the two different ways in which elites were commissioning art.

The third paragraph doesn't offer additional evidence for any of this; it just pivots into the idea that T & Co. are using the 2nd way, and the 2nd way has some sketchy assumptions built into it.

choices.text: draw a definitive conclusion from the claims made in the second paragraph
choices.explanation:
The second paragraph just outlined what the two ways are. The third paragraph explained that the second way, which is what T & Co. prefer, comes with a couple underlying requirements.

To draw a definitive conclusion from claims would fit better if the 2nd paragraph were laying out some facts and then the 3rd paragraph sounded like the author giving us one big takeaway.

But the 2nd paragraph isn't quite evidence for a conclusion. It's just some background clarification. And the 3rd paragraph isn't providing our author's definitive conclusion -- it's a setup for the 4th and 5th paragraph, in which we sequentially undermine assumption #1 and assumption #2 of T & Co's methodology.

questions.prompt: The author mentions "Raphael's frescoes in the Vatican apartments" (last sentence of the second paragraph) for which one of the following reasons?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipating Answer
explanationBlocks.body:
*Why* did the author discuss these frescoes? The purpose of an example is almost always revealed by the idea that sets it up. The frescoes are brought up at the end of the 2nd paragraph as an example of "the second way".

So the author mentioned the frescoes *to illustrate a case in which art was commissioned in order to express the ideals of the person paying for it*.

choices.text: to provide an example that illustrates the understanding of elitism in art favored by sociohistorical critics
choices.explanation: We wanted "an example of *the second way*", and *the second way* is the understanding of elitism in art favored by T and other sociohistorical critics, so this answer seems accurate.

choices.text: to illustrate the influence of religion on the historical development of art
choices.explanation:
When we're asked about the *purpose* of a detail, there's usually a trap answer that's too focused on the *what*, not the *why*. Yes, the frescoes are an example of religious art, but the author didn't bring them up to make a broad point about religious art.

Instead she brought them up to give an example of "art that reflects the ideals of the elite" (whether those ideals are religious or secular is beside the point)

choices.text: to present an example of the most common type of relationship between a patron and an artist
choices.explanation:
We wanted "an example of *the second way*". Is the second way the *most common* way?

We don't know. We only know that T & Co. prefer to think of the relationship that way, but our author never quantifies whether the first way or second way was more common.

choices.text: to show how an artist can subvert the ideals of the patron
choices.explanation: This is an example of the artist *expressing and mirroring* the ideals of the patron.

choices.text: to show that there are cases of artist/patron relationships that do not fit the pattern preferred by sociohistorical critics
choices.explanation: We wanted "an example of *the second way*", and the second way is the artist/patron relationship that *does* fit the pattern preferred by sociohistorical critics.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that Matthew Arnold would be most likely to identify which one of the following as the primary reason why, historically, people in the middle class became patrons of the arts?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body: All we know from Matthew Arnold as it relates to the middle class is that they are "Philistines, obsessed with respectability".

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipating Answer
explanationBlocks.body: Arnold calls the middle class Philistines obsessed with respectability. A desire for a respected reputation therefore fits his characterization. The passage does not require an outside social theory of the bourgeoisie or establish that only aristocrats' approval mattered.

choices.text: a belief in the importance of the arts to society as a whole
choices.explanation: We can't get from "philistine obsessed with respectability" to "I believe the arts are important to society as a whole".

choices.text: a dislike for the kind of art typically sponsored by the aristocracy
choices.explanation: Arnold's characterization concerns their desire for respectability. It does not establish that dislike of aristocratic art was their primary motive, or that they necessarily shared aristocratic taste.

choices.text: a belief that patronage would ultimately prove profitable
choices.explanation: We can't get from "philistine obsessed with respectability" to "I believe that by paying for this art, I will ultimately make money".

choices.text: a realization that patronage ensures the production of high-quality art
choices.explanation: There's nothing in "philistine obsessed with respectability" that sounds like "I believe that if I pay for art, it will ****100% guarantee**** high-quality art".

choices.text: a desire to establish a reputation as a patron of the arts
choices.explanation:
This is our closest match for "philistine obsessed with respectability". We have to understand that *obsessed with respectability* means *obsessed with how others see you*.

And "reputation" is all about how others see you.

passages.title: Clay Tokens
passages.text:
Hundreds of clay tablets marked in cuneiform have been found in excavations of the Sumerian city of Uruk (in present-day Iraq). Though the tablets date from roughly 3000 B.C., the writing on them uses relatively few pictographs; instead, numerous abstract symbols are used. The sign for “sheep”, for example, is not an image of a sheep, but rather a circled cross, while the sign for “metal” is a crescent with five lines. Because of its early date, this seemingly sudden appearance of such abstract writing has long puzzled researchers. At the same time, among prepottery clay artifacts found at archaeological sites along the Jordan and nearby rivers are thousands of small, hand-modeled tokens of fired clay, some dating to before 4000 B.C. Often ignored by archaeologists—some concluded without evidence that they were amulets or game pieces—the tokens are identified by Denise Schmandt-Besserat in her book *Before Writing* (1992) as overlooked predecessors to the written word.

The earliest of the tokens were simple in form—small cones, spheres, and pyramids—and they were often inscribed. In 1966, a hollow tablet containing several of these tokens was discovered, and more than 100 additional tablets, which are now recognized as sealed envelopes of clay, have since been found. Later envelopes are also inscribed with impressions of tokens in the outer clay, signaling exactly what each envelope contained. Noting that these inscriptions are clearly traceable to later, known inscriptions of farm products, Schmandt-Besserat theorizes that the envelopes contained official records of villagers’ contributions to temple-based grain and livestock pools. After 4000 B.C., hundreds of new token forms developed, as a rise in industry boosted the token system. Many forms are figurative, such as bowls or jars with handles, suggesting that villagers’ crafts were becoming more diversified and sophisticated.

The token system, essentially a system of three- dimensional nouns, was replaced in about 3100 B.C. by a system of marks on clay tablets. A few centuries later, this latter system was to display the first use of numerals, where simple marks coded the concepts of one, two, and so forth. The eventual evolution of this system into mature writing, Schmandt-Besserat suggests, can be seen in the following example: At first it took two ovoid tokens to record two jars of oil. A little later, it took two markings on a clay tablet to achieve this—one mark, using the outline of the old token, to record the customary unit measure for oil, the jarful, and a second mark to convey the numeral: two oil jars. Eventually, it took three signs on the tablet, one for the numeral 2, one for the standard jarful, and a new symbol that denoted oil itself. With three such signs, an abstract and flexible written form had arrived.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The origins and evolution of writing in ancient Mesopotamia, focusing on how clay tokens led to abstract cuneiform writing.

**Framework**

Theme / Example

**Main Point**

Ancient clay tokens served as precursors to written language in Mesopotamia, and over time, this token system transformed into increasingly abstract and flexible writing forms like cuneiform.
**The Most Valuable Sentence:** The passage’s main point is neatly summed up in the transition of tokens to written marks—especially the lines, "The token system, essentially a system of three-dimensional nouns, was replaced in about 3100 B.C. by a system of marks on clay tablets ... Eventually, it took three signs on the tablet ... an abstract and flexible written form had arrived." (Paragraph 3)

**P1: Discovery of Early Writing and the Puzzle of Abstract Symbols**

Researchers find ancient clay tablets from Uruk, dated around 3000 B.C., with abstract, non-pictorial cuneiform writing—which is unusual for such an early date. Archaeologists often ignored even older clay tokens found nearby, but Denise Schmandt-Besserat argues these tokens were actually early precursors to writing.

**P2: Description and Evolution of Tokens into Record-Keeping**

Early tokens were simple in shape and sometimes inscribed, later found inside sealed "envelope" tablets. These inscribed tokens probably served as records of agricultural contributions to temples. After 4000 B.C., more sophisticated token shapes appeared, reflecting increased complexity in crafts and record-keeping.

**P3: Transition from Token System to Written Language**

Eventually, the system shifted from three-dimensional tokens to marks on clay tablets (about 3100 B.C.), allowing for record-keeping using drawn symbols instead of physical tokens. This evolved into full-fledged writing, with separate signs for numerals, objects, and even abstract ideas—leading to a more flexible and advanced written language system.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Main Point = Central Topic + Purpose/Framework

The central topic of this passage is Schmandt-Besserat's book *Before Writing*, which discusses clay artifacts from 4000 B.C. that may be predecessors to the written word.

Why is the author writing about the book? Does he accept its conclusions? Does he challenge them? Something else?

The author never really makes any appearance. The 2nd and 3rd paragraphs basically unfurl the main details and takeaways of the book, so we would consider this a *Highlight Noteworthy* passage. Our author is just presenting this book, because it makes an interesting argument.

So our main point would be the main point of the book, which seems to be that "the evolution of these clay tokens in 4000 B.C. to a system of marks on clay tablets is a very early example of *mature writing*, an abstract and flexible written form."

choices.text: Based on her analysis of inscription-bearing clay envelopes containing tokens dating to roughly 4000 B.C., Schmandt-Besserat concludes that this system of tokens eventually evolved into an abstract written language.
choices.explanation:
The main clause here is that *Schmandt-Besserat concludes that this system of tokens eventually evolved into an abstract written language*.

That seems like what we were looking for. At the end of the first paragraph, we hear the thesis of the book summarized as "Schmandt-Besserat identifies these tokens as overlooked predecessors to the written word".

At the very end of the passage, Schmandt-Besserat is saying, "Check it out -- with these three signs, an abstract and flexible written form had arrived!"

Since the main clause is solid, we would verify the details of the warm-up clause, but it looks accurate. She analyzed clay envelopes that date back to 4000 B.C.

choices.text: The discovery of clay tablets bearing inscriptions representing the tokens they contain confirms the belief of Schmandt-Besserat that these tokens served to designate the products given by villagers to their temples.
choices.explanation:
The main clause here is
*The discovery of clay tablets confirms the belief of Schmandt-Besserat that these tokens served to designate the products given by villagers*.

That's not the main takeaway. She didn't write her book to say, "Check it out, world -- these tokens really DID serve to designate the products given by villagers to their temples". That was a small idea from the 2nd paragraph.

The big idea is, "Check it out, world -- these tokens might be our earliest example yet of people developing a written language!"

choices.text: Inscription-bearing clay envelopes containing tokens discovered in modern Iraq have provided Schmandt-Besserat with the evidence required to resolve the puzzlement of archaeologists over the sudden appearance of sophisticated crafts.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: puzzlement over crafts
choices.explanation:
The main clause here is
*The clay envelopes have provided Schmandt-Besserat with evidence needed to resolve the puzzlement of archaeologists over the sudden appearance of sophisticated crafts.*

The passage never says that any archaeologists are puzzled at the sudden appearance of sophisticated crafts.

We are told that they have long been puzzled by the "seemingly sudden appearance of **such abstract writing**" as that found on the clay tablets found in Uruk.

choices.text: The inscriptions found on clay envelopes containing small clay tokens have enabled Schmandt-Besserat to formulate a more detailed picture of the way in which a simple system of three-dimensional nouns evolved into modern languages.
choices.tag: Unsupported Causal Claim: evolved into modern
choices.explanation:
The main clause here is
*The inscriptions on the clay envelopes have enabled Schmandt-Besserat to formulate a more detailed picture of the way in which a simple system of 3D nouns evolved into modern languages.*

That's fairly close to the right main point. It's weird to say that the clay tablets enabled "a *more* detailed" picture, because nothing in the passage suggests that there was already a picture developed that this is refining. The passage seemed to be saying, "She thinks she just discovered the earlier example of written language!"

But the most offending part of this answer is the notion that this simple system of 3D nouns evolved into modern languages. We have no support for that causal claim.

Modern languages might have evolved from a totally different starting point. The passage is merely saying that this may be the earliest example of anything resembling a written language.

choices.text: The discovery of inscription-bearing clay envelopes containing small tokens confirms Schmandt-Besserat’s hypothesis that a language becomes increasingly abstract as the arts and crafts of the people who use the language become more abstract.
choices.explanation:
The main clause here is
*The discovery of clay envelopes confirms Schmandt-Besserat's hypothesis that a language becomes increasingly abstract as the arts and crafts become more abstract.*

The passage never insinuated this causal connection that as crafts become more abstract, it causes the language to become more abstract.

In fact, the passage never even talks about crafts becoming more abstract. It just talks about them becoming more diverse and sophisticated.

Schmandt-Besserat's discovery/hypothesis is simply, "The stuff these guys were doing with these clay envelopes is basically an abstract and flexible written language!"

questions.prompt: With which one of the following statements about the society in which the clay tokens were used would Schmandt-Besserat be most likely to agree?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Are there any references in the text to the *society* where these tokens were found?

From the 1st paragraph, we know this society ...
- lived along the Jordan river and other nearby rivers

From the 2nd paragraph, we know this society ...
- had temple-based grain and livestock pools, that villagers would contribute to
- had a boom in industry that coincided with a proliferation of token types, which also coincided with more diverse and sophisticated crafts being made.

From the 3rd paragraph, we know this society ...
- evolved its way of keeping track of things like jars of oil

We have a lot of potential Support sentences, so let's use our aversion to language that is Too Strong / Too Specific / Unknown Comparison / Out of Scope, to distance ourselves from some of these choices, so that we have time to research Supporting Text for the contenders.

choices.text: Society members’ trade and other economic activities were managed by a strong centralized governmental authority.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: strong central govt.
choices.explanation:
We can support that there was ****some**** central organization, because the 2nd paragraph's depiction of villagers contributing livestock and grain to a community pool speaks to some level of collectivism and central organization.

But it's identified as ****temple-based****, not governmental authority. And it's too broad even to say that these temples managed "trade ****and other activities****".

choices.text: Religious rituals were probably less important to the society’s members than agriculture and trade were.
choices.explanation: Nothing in the passage ranks religion vs. agriculture vs. trade, in terms of what this society would have found more or less important.

choices.text: Society members regarded whatever was produced by any individual as the common property of all.
choices.explanation:
We can support that there was ****some**** collectivism, because of the 2nd paragraph's depiction of villagers contributing livestock and grain to a community pool.

But we only heard that grain and livestock were somewhat treated as communal property.

It's a huge leap from that to saying that ****whatever**** was produced by ****any**** person was thus the common property of ****all****.

choices.text: The society eventually came to regard the clay tokens as redundant.
choices.explanation:
The 3rd paragraph tells us in its first sentence that the token system was ****replaced**** in about 3100 B.C.

In the middle of the last paragraph, we get a little more support for redundancy, as they describe how ...

*at first* ... it took two ovoid ****tokens**** to record two jars of oil
*a little later* ... it took two markings on clay tablet (using the outline of the ****old**** token)

Since the token system was replaced by clay tablets, the *old* tokens lived on in terms of the meaning of their familiar outlines, but it would have been redundant to ****also**** have the tokens.

This is, of course, a little speculative. Maybe there was some utility in having the tokens for some other purpose that we weren't told about.

But this is the best available answer. We have more textual support for this than for any other contender.

choices.text: Without a readily available supply of raw clay, the society could not have developed a system of representation that used tokens.
choices.tag: Too Strong: without clay, could not have
choices.explanation:
Nothing in the passage indicates that clay was the only plausible option for what to make tokens out of. But this answer is acting like having a token system ****required**** having clay.

They could have carved tokens into wood or stone, for all we know.

questions.prompt: The passage states that the writing on clay tablets found in Uruk

choices.text: was not deciphered by archaeologists until 1992
used relatively few pictographic symbols
eventually evolved into a more abstract and flexible linguistic system
transcribed a language that was commonly spoken along the Jordan and nearby rivers
transcribed a language that was much older than archaeologists would have expected

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the token system

choices.text: was eventually abandoned because it was not capable of representing quantity and other abstractions
came to designate a broad range of objects as the crafts of the people who used it became more diverse and sophisticated
could be understood only because some tokens were inscribed with symbols known to represent agricultural products
was originally thought by most archaeologists to have had a primarily religious function
became physically unwieldy and cumbersome as its users’ agricultural products became more diverse

questions.prompt: By characterizing certain cuneiform inscriptions on the clay tablets found in Uruk as “abstract” (middle of the first paragraph) the author most likely means that

choices.text: the meaning of the inscriptions is obscure and hard for linguists to decipher
the inscriptions are meant to represent intangible concepts
the inscriptions do not resemble what they designate
the inscriptions refer to general categories rather than specific things
the terms represented by the inscriptions were more ceremonial in nature than most daily speech was

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the discussion of clay tokens in the second paragraph that

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Since clay tokens are the main topic of the passage, we wouldn't be expecting to find one specific line in the 2nd paragraph that talked about clay tokens, but it's still probably worth a quick sweep to remind ourselves what sort of ideas *are* in the Support Window.

- earliest tokens were simple shapes, sometimes inscribed
- early envelopes of tokens were unlabeled, later envelopes were labeled
- the tokens seemed to record how much grain or livestock a villager had contributed to community pools
- after 4000 B.C., a rise in industry coincided with a proliferation of new token types as well as new handicraft designs.

choices.text: there were many tokens that designated more than one type of item
choices.tag: Out of Scope: designated more than one
choices.explanation: We don't hear about any token, in the 2nd paragraph, that stood for more than one idea.

choices.text: nonagricultural goods and products came to be preferred as contributions to temple-based pools
choices.explanation: The passage identifies grain and livestock as contributions but gives no comparison showing that nonagricultural products became preferred. Evidence of agricultural contributions does not by itself establish an opposite preference either.

choices.text: some later tokens were less abstract than some earlier ones
choices.explanation:
The earliest tokens (at the beginning of the 2nd paragraph) are just cones, spheres, or pyramids, sometimes inscribed, sometimes blank.

If a pyramid represents livestock, for example, that's pretty ****abstract**** (i.e. nonrepresentational).

Meanwhile, the last sentence in the 2nd paragraph tell us that the forms emerging in the post 4000 B.C. explosion of tokens are ****figurative**** -- one has the figure of a bowl. The other has a jar with handles.

That's more representational, less abstract. The later token is just showing you, "jar with handles", not asking you to remember that "sphere + two lines on it = jar with handles".

choices.text: the storage and transportation of liquids were among the most important tasks performed by the token system’s users
choices.tag: Too Strong: most important / Out of Scope: transporting of liquids
choices.explanation:
The "transporting of liquids" seems like it comes out of left field, but I guess they're playing off the fact that we mentioned bowls and jars with handles, both of which could store or transport liquids.

Just because the author pulled two random examples that happen to both be crafts that can hold liquid, we can't assume that storing/moving liquid was among the ****most important**** tasks the people in this society performed.

choices.text: the token system was as abstract and flexible as later written languages
choices.tag: Unknown Comparison / Too Strong: equally abstract/flexible
choices.explanation:
Nothing in the 2nd paragraph discusses ****later written languages****, so we should be able to get rid of this just because it's clearly out of our Support Window.

But even at the end of the 3rd where we talk about the eventual tablet inscriptions being an abstract and flexible written form, we aren't comparing it to later written languages and making the bold claim that this three-sign system was ****as abstract and as flexible**** as later languages.

questions.prompt: With which one of the following statements regarding the sign for “sheep” (third sentence of the first paragraph) would the author of the passage be most likely to agree?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Does our author have any moments of attitude or rhetorical device in the early going of this first paragraph, where "sheep" is mentioned?

There is a rhetorical device right after the word "sheep": *for example.* If the sign for "sheep" is an example, it's an example of what was said right before it -- an abstract symbol.

The sign was a circled cross, so we can infer the author believes that a circled cross is "an abstract symbol" for a sheep.

The following sentence also seems to have a little author pizazz:
*Because* *of its early date, this* *****seemingly***** *sudden appearance of such abstract writing has long puzzled researchers.*

"Most likely to agree" questions love to use moments in the passage where the author's voice comes through subtly through the use of adverbs, such as *seemingly, regrettably, conveniently, importantly*, etc.

What does that adverb add to the meaning of that sentence?

Seeing an abstract symbol for sheep in 3000 B.C. ****seemed**** like a sudden appearance of abstract writing ... ****(but it wasn't a sudden appearance)****.

Does our author think that the sign for sheep was ****not**** a puzzling, sudden appearance of abstract writing in 3000 B.C.?

Yes, that's accurate. After all, the point of this early introduction of the passage is that the ****real**** origin story of abstract writing might be 1000 years earlier, with these clay tokens from 4000 B.C.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Ultimately, we just want to pick whatever answer we feel is most supportable by the text, whether it's important or minor, whether it's our prediction or something else.

But my spidey sense would think that they're going to use that ****seemingly**** as the launching pad for what the author's voice is invisibly trying to convey there.

choices.text: It could have been replaced without loss of significance by any other sign that was not already being used for something else.
choices.explanation:
Hahaha, my prediction was WAY off! I would have never predicted this wording. And that's fine. We can aspire to predict but still realize that we're ultimately at the mercy of what answers we're offered.

This answer is not supported much by any single sentence in the passage, it's just supported by two things:

1. we know the author considers the sign for "sheep" to be an abstract symbol

2. our common sense would tells us that if you're picking an abstract symbol to represent something, it doesn't matter what it is.

If I'm going to label grape jelly with a lightning bolt, it would just as make sense to label it with a pyramid. It's just an abstract symbol that people will learn, by convention, to associate with grape jelly.

It always feels unnerving (to me) to pick answer choices that involve adding so much common sense, but modern RC will make us do that sometimes.

choices.text: The sign gets its meaning in a radically different way from the way in which the cuneiform sign for “metal” gets its meaning.
choices.explanation:
The author is actually presenting the sign for *sheep* and the one for *metal* as two ****similar**** examples of highly abstract symbols.

The "while" being used there is not the *contrast*-while, but rather the *simultaneous*-while.

Ben cooked dinner, while Kyle set the table.

choices.text: The way in which it represents its meaning resulted from the fact that sheep are an agricultural commodity rather than a product of human industry.
choices.explanation:
We have no idea how a circled cross came to mean "sheep". There's nothing in the passage that suggests that because sheep are an agricultural commodity rather than a product of human industry, that allowed people to see how a circled cross would represent the meaning "sheep".

This is sort of the opposite of the correct answer. This answer is making it seem like the symbol for sheep is meaningful and has a causal backstory. The correct answer is recognizing that the author's point is that the sign for sheep is totally arbitrary, just an abstract symbol.

choices.text: The way in which it represents its meaning was not the subject of scientific scrutiny prior to that given it by Schmandt-Besserat.
choices.tag: Too Strong: not until / Unsupported: S-B connection
choices.explanation:
This is a very harshly worded claim, and not only do we not know, "****no one**** prior to Schmandt-Besserat ever gave scientific scrutiny to how the sheep sign represented sheep", we don't even know if Schmandt-Besserat ever gave this sign scientific scrutiny.

She was studying clay tokens near the Jordan river from 4000 B.C.

This sheep sign is from present-day Irag from 3000 B.C.

choices.text: The abstract nature of the sign reveals a great deal about the political life of the people who used the language expressed by cuneiform writing.
choices.tag: Too Strong: reveals a great deal / Out of Scope: political life
choices.explanation:
The author would probably say the abstract nature of the sign reveals that humans already had the abstract writing precursors to the written language by 3000 B.C. (if not earlier).

But the author hasn't drawn any connections between the abstract sign and the ****political life**** of the people who used cuneiform.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Schmandt-Besserat's theory mentioned in the fourth sentence of the second paragraph?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body:
In the 2nd paragraph, we've got ourselves a Curious Fact:
*what's the deal with these envelopes of clay, filled with tokens, that are inscribed on the outside to show what the envelope contains?*

Schmandt-Beserat's Explanation:
*These envelopes were keeping the tally of how much each villager had contributed to a collective, temple-organized pool of grain and livestock.*

Her evidence:
*the inscriptions on the envelopes are similar to later inscriptions, which we know referred to farm products*

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
If we're going to weaken her theory, we'll either need an

****- Alternate Explanation**** for the inscriptions / envelopes / tokens,
or we'll need something that
****- Hurts the Plausibility**** of the story that these envelopes were "bank accounts" held by the local temple, keeping track of whether villagers were paying their fair share towards the communal supply of grain and meat.

choices.text: The more than 100 clay envelopes discovered at archaeological sites along the Jordan come in many different dimensions, thicknesses, and styles of composition.
choices.explanation:
This is the classic, wishy-washy answer we see on Strengthen / Weaken questions:
- things occur
- things fluctuate
- things differ
- some of the envelopes were heavy, some were light

The fact that these envelopes came in a wide variety of shapes and thicknesses doesn't make any difference to whether or not the *inscriptions* are connected to temple-based tallies of villagers contributions.

choices.text: It was customary for villagers who performed services for another person to receive in return a record of a promise of agricultural products or crafted objects as compensation.
choices.explanation:
This provides an ****Alternate Explanation**** for the clay envelopes:
*maybe the envelopes were sort of a payment contract*.

I clean out your gutters, you promise me some meat in the fall and give me an envelope with an inscription of the agricultural product (meat) you're promising me?

We know that LSAT's preferred move when weakening a causal hypothesis is to provide an alternate explanation, but this is a very thinly suggested alternate explanation. Pretty tough to hear what they were going for.

It's very important that we are listening charitably for a possible alternate way to explain these envelopes, so that "****a record**** of a promise of agricultural products" sticks out as LSAT vaguely alluding to the envelopes.

choices.text: The tablets marked in cuneiform dating after 3000 B.C. do not seem to function as records of villagers’ contributions to a temple-based pool of goods.
choices.explanation: This concerns cuneiform tablets after 3000 B.C., not the earlier token-containing envelopes whose purpose the theory explains. A later change of use does not provide the direct competing explanation for those earlier records that B offers.

choices.text: There is no archaeological evidence suggesting that the tokens in use from about 4000 B.C. to 3100 B.C. were necessarily meant to be placed in clay envelopes.
choices.explanation: Absence of evidence that tokens necessarily belonged in envelopes is not evidence that any particular token did not belong there. The theory concerns the function of the envelopes that did contain tokens; it does not require every token in the later period to have been made for an envelope.

choices.text: Villagers were required not only to contribute goods to central pools but also to contribute labor, which was regularly accounted for.
choices.explanation: This actually ****increases**** the plausibility of the story S-B is telling, in which the community is expected to contribute to a temple-organized pool of grain and livestock.

passages.title: Chlorofluorocarbons and the Ozone
passages.text:
By 1970 it was well established that ultraviolet light from the sun contributes to skin cancer. Fortunately, much of the sun’s most damaging ultraviolet radiation is screened out by a thin, diffuse layer of ozone—a toxic form of oxygen—in the stratosphere, 10 to 25 miles above the earth’s surface.

During the 1970s, however, public policy makers worldwide were alerted to the fragility of the ozone layer through the pioneering research and advocacy of two Nobel Prize-winning scientists, Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland. In the absence of pollutants, stratospheric ozone concentrations should remain stable over time, with natural production and destruction of the gas in rough equilibrium. Molina and Rowland showed how manufactured chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)—highly volatile chemicals, millions of tons of which had been used each year in products such as aerosol sprays and refrigerants—chemically attack and deplete the ozone layer, diminishing its effectiveness as a shield against ultraviolet radiation. Studying two freon gases—types of CFCs—they observed that, when released into the lower atmosphere (troposphere), these gases slowly diffuse upward into the stratosphere. There, subjected to massive ultraviolet radiation, they break down into their constituent elements, including chlorine. The resulting increase in the concentration of chlorine in the stratosphere is devastating to the ozone layer. Chlorine and ozone chemically react in a way that both destroys the ozone and regenerates the chlorine atoms. As a result of this chemical reaction, each chlorine atom could destroy as many as 100,000 ozone molecules before becoming inactive.

In 1974 the two scientists estimated that the atmosphere contained the accumulation of five years of global CFC production. This meant that, given the rate of diffusion and breakdown of CFCs in the atmosphere, the depletion of the ozone layer would continue for years, if not decades, even if the production and use of CFCs were to cease immediately. Recognizing this as a pressing environmental threat, Molina and Rowland became public advocates for a prompt and proportionate public policy response. As a result, Molina was invited to testify before the U.S. Congress and was later appointed to the U.S. National Science Foundation Committee on Fluorocarbon Technology Assessment.

Predictably, the work of Molina and Rowland and their advocacy of dramatic policy changes were subjected to attacks by critics, especially scientists with ties to the CFC industry. However, over time their views were corroborated, especially by the discovery of a hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica, and this led to the development of an international agreement (the Montreal Protocol of 1987) to ban the production of ozone-depleting gases. In North America, CFCs were banned in the late 1970s, leading to a transformation in packaging for consumer spray products and the development of more environmentally friendly refrigerant chemicals.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The effects of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) on ozone depletion and the resulting public policy response.

**Framework**

Problem / Solution

**Main Point**

Molina and Rowland discovered that CFCs deplete the ozone layer, which protects us from cancer-causing ultraviolet radiation, prompting international policy change to control these pollutants.
"The resulting increase in the concentration of chlorine in the stratosphere is devastating to the ozone layer... each chlorine atom could destroy as many as 100,000 ozone molecules before becoming inactive." (Paragraph 2)
This is wrapped up in Paragraph 4, where it summarizes the outcome: "their views were corroborated... and this led to the development of an international agreement (the Montreal Protocol of 1987) to ban the production of ozone-depleting gases."

**P1: Importance of the Ozone Layer**

By 1970, it was understood that ultraviolet radiation from the sun can cause skin cancer, but thankfully Earth's ozone layer filters out much of this harmful radiation.

**P2: Discovery of the Ozone Problem**

Scientists Molina and Rowland revealed that man-made chemicals called CFCs, found in products like aerosols and refrigerants, break down in the upper atmosphere and release chlorine, which destroys ozone. A single chlorine atom can wipe out thousands of ozone molecules.

**P3: The Lasting Threat and Call to Action**

Their research showed that even if we stopped using CFCs immediately, the chemicals already present would keep damaging ozone for many years. Molina and Rowland pushed for urgent public policies to address this environmental danger, leading to political attention and involvement in research committees.

**P4: Policy Response and Confirmation**

Initially, critics (often those connected to industry) opposed their findings, but more scientific evidence—like the ozone hole over Antarctica—confirmed the risk. This led to global agreements banning CFCs, starting with North America and culminating in the Montreal Protocol, which also spurred the development of safer alternatives for consumer goods.

questions.prompt: The information in the passage most helps to answer which one of the following questions?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: There's no way to get ourselves prepared for this type of question. As we find keywords in each answer choice, we might consider doing a Ctrl + F search so that we can find which ever area of the text contains *any* info relating to that topic, and thus assess whether that area of text provides an answer to the question.

choices.text: What laboratory experiments were conducted by Molina or Rowland in their research on CFCs?
choices.explanation:
In the 2nd paragraph, we're told that M & R studied two types of CFCs and observed how they behave in the lower atmosphere and stratosphere.

But that sounds more like a field observation. We don't hear anything about **laboratory** experiments.

choices.text: What was the estimated concentration of CFCs in the atmosphere in 1987?
choices.explanation: 1987 is only mentioned once in the final paragraph and there's nothing in there that spells out any concentration of CFCs.

choices.text: In what year did Molina testify before the U.S. Congress?
choices.tag: Out of Scope: year of testimony
choices.explanation:
We know from the 3rd paragraph that Molina and Rowland "**became** public advocates" starting around 1974 and that Molina was invited to testify before Congress.

But we don't know if that was in 1974 or one of the following years.

choices.text: Does any chemical that does not contain chlorine contribute to the destruction of ozone molecules?
choices.explanation:
The only destroyer of ozone molecules we hear about is chlorine. There may be others; there might not be, but we can't say.

The passage never told us that "**only** chlorine can contribute to the destruction of ozone molecules".

choices.text: Which constituent element of CFCs is most damaging to ozone?
choices.explanation:
The most damaging ingredient is chlorine!

We're told that, "once in the stratosphere, CFCs break down into their constituent elements, including chlorine. The resulting increase in the concentration of chlorine in the stratosphere is **devastating** to the ozone layer (because each chlorine atom could destroy as many as 100,000 ozone molecules."

Nothing in that text specifically spells out that chlorine is the most damaging part of a CFC, but it's highly, highly suggested.

If there were some other ingredient in CFCs that was even worse for the ozone layer than chlorine is, wouldn't this passage have mentioned it? It would be highly relevant to the conversation. It would go very much against common sense that the author would fail to mention a part of CFC's that is even **more devastating** to the ozone layer.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the conclusions of Molina and Rowland concerning the long-term effects of CFCs in the stratosphere?

choices.text: The hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica continued to grow for years after CFC emissions had almost ceased.
Other manufactured chemicals have been found to diffuse upward into the stratosphere when released into the troposphere.
Ozone has been shown to react more violently with chlorine than with many other chemicals.
Many scientists who in the 1970s were highly critical of the research methods of Molina and Rowland have come to accept the soundness of their methods.
Current CFC levels in the troposphere suggest that not all nations currently abide by the Montreal Protocol.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
There are no *Clue Words* in the question stem, so we just head to the answers. On the first pass we'll try to distance ourselves from any answers that seem to have toxic qualities:

- Too Strong
- Unknown Broad Comparison
- Out of Scope
- Goes Against Passage
- Unsupported Causal Relationship

If we see an answer with soft, safe language, we'll see if we can find supporting lines to clinch picking it.

choices.text: Little or no ozone destruction occurs naturally in the stratosphere unless chlorine is present.
choices.explanation:
We are being told that chlorine is terribly damaging to ozone in the stratosphere.

We're never told **it's the only thing** that destroys ozone in the stratosphere. This is playing the age old trick of acting like "Only Thing *Mentioned* = Only Thing".

We're actually told in the 2nd sentence of the 2nd paragraph that in its natural state, the ozone layer was "natural production **and destruction** in rough equilibrium". So there are other things that destroy ozone, but they are offset by natural production of more ozone.

choices.text: Skin cancers occur primarily because of excessive absorption of ultraviolet light.
choices.explanation:
We are told in the first sentence that UV radiation **contributes** to skin cancer.

We're never told **it's the #1 source** skin cancer. This is acting like like "the only cause of skin cancer *Mentioned* = the #1 cause of skin cancer".

choices.text: Few chemicals besides CFCs can result in the release of chlorine in the upper atmosphere.
choices.explanation:
We are told that CFC's can break down and result in the release of chlorine in the upper atmosphere.

We're never told **it's one of the only things** that can result in chlorine in the upper atmosphere.

Just because the passage only mentions CFC's releasing chlorine doesn't mean we get to act like CFC's are "one of only a few things" that release chlorine.

choices.text: Regulating the use of CFCs contributes indirectly to lowering the incidence of skin cancer.
choices.explanation:
Regulating the use of CFC's contributes to keeping the ozone layer as a functional shield against incoming UV light from the sun.

UV light from the sun contributes to skin cancer.

So this is giving us a little causal chain:

*Regulate → stronger → less UV → less skin*
*CFC's ozone layer gets thru cancer*

When we say "A causes B, which causes C", then we can say that A **directly** caused B and **indirectly** caused C.

choices.text: The upward flow of CFCs into the stratosphere occurs mainly in Antarctica.
choices.explanation: The passage locates an ozone hole over Antarctica but does not locate most upward diffusion of CFCs there. The general diffusion description in paragraph 2 gives no geographic concentration. No speculative explanation involving atmospheric thickness is needed.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, the information yielded by which one of the following experiments would be most useful in determining whether a particular chemical could replace CFCs without damaging the ozone layer?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
To mentally prep ourselves for these answers, let's remind ourselves how CFC's damage the ozone layer:

They break down into constituent atoms in the stratosphere, including chlorine. And chlorine messes up the ozone layer by reacting with ozone in a way that destroys tons of ozone molecules.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
So let's look for an answer saying something like,
"let's find out whether this substitute would break down into constituent atoms in the stratosphere / let's find out whether any of those constituent atoms would react with ozone in a way that would destroy tons of ozone molecules"

choices.text: testing to see whether the chemical is capable of reacting with forms of oxygen other than ozone
choices.explanation: We want to test whether the chemical would react with ozone, not stuff *other than* ozone.

choices.text: testing to see whether the chemical, when released into the lower atmosphere, would react with other chemicals commonly found there
choices.explanation: We want to test whether the chemical would react with ozone in the stratosphere (upper atmosphere), not whether it reacts with other stuff in the lower atmosphere.

choices.text: testing the chemical to determine whether it would chemically react with chlorine
choices.explanation: The intended replacement is for CFCs, not for chlorine as an environmental substance. The relevant risk is whether the replacement or its breakdown products damage ozone, rather than whether they react with chlorine.

choices.text: testing to see what chemical properties the chemical or its constituent elements share with chlorine
choices.explanation:
We want to test whether the chemical would react with ozone the way chlorine reacted with ozone (by destroying the ozone).

If we can see whether this potential replacement has chemical properties in common with chlorine that would cause it to react with ozone the same way, then we'll get the answer we're seeking.

This answer is designed to be un-tempting by only talking about *part* of what we would want / need to know to make our assessment.

We would not only need to know what chemical properties this potential replacement shares with chlorine, but we would also need to know which chemical properties of chlorine cause it to destroy ozone. But presumably the chemists doing chemical testing do know such stuff.

Even though an answer to this question wouldn't give us the final verdict on its own, it's still a more valuable question to answer than any of the other answer choices.

choices.text: testing the chemical to see if it would break down into its components when subjected to ultraviolet radiation
choices.tag: Not as Helpful as Correct Answer
choices.explanation:
This is tempting. If we tested the chemical and found out that it didn't break down into its components, would that show that it's harmless in the ozone layer?

Not necessarily. It might not need to break down into constituent elements in order to react adversely with ozone.

If it *does* break down into constituent parts, does that mean it would be harmful in the ozone layer?

Not necessarily. Its constituent parts might not have any adverse reactions with ozone.

Even though answering this question would be somewhat useful, it leaves us farther from a final verdict than would answering the question in (D). Ultimately what we care about the most is whether this replacement would react adversely with ozone.

The question posed by (D) potentially reveals that answer, whether the replacement chemical breaks down into constituent elements or not, because the language of (D) covers the reactive possibilities of the replacement molecule as well as the reactive possibilities of the constituent atoms in the replacement.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
There's no way for us to anticipate where in the passage the correct answer will be coming from, so we'll just consider each answer and look up the details to see if we can support it.

Trap answers will usually have one or more of these features:
- Too Strong/Specific
- Unknown Comparison
- Unmentioned Concept
- Contradicts passage

choices.text: No refrigerant chemicals other than CFCs had been discovered when Molina and Rowland suggested that CFC production cease.
choices.explanation:
We were told that some CFCs were refrigerants.

This answer is saying that "all known refrigerants are CFCs". We can't support that anywhere in the passage.

choices.text: Refrigerant chemicals developed as substitutes for CFCs after 1987 release fewer chlorine atoms into the stratosphere than CFCs do.
choices.explanation: The passage links CFC harm to chlorine release, including destruction of ozone molecules, and describes later refrigerants as more environmentally friendly replacements. In that context, reduced chlorine release is the supported improvement. A chlorine atom may destroy up to 100,000 ozone molecules, not 100,000 oxygen atoms.

choices.text: CFCs were originally used in refrigeration components because they provided the most energy-efficient means of refrigeration.
choices.tag: Too Strong: most / Unsupported Causal Relationship
choices.explanation:
We were never told why CFC's were originally used. Maybe it was because they provided the most energy-efficient means of refrigeration.

Maybe they provided the 2nd most energy-efficient means but they smelled better, or they were easier to make cheaply. We have no idea.

choices.text: The Montreal Protocol led to the cessation of CFC production in North America.
choices.explanation: The final two sentences suggest the opposite of this. The Montreal Protocol wasn't until 1987, but we're told that North America ceased CFC production in the late 1970s, when CFC's were banned.

choices.text: Some of the refrigerant chemicals being manufactured today contain chemicals known to be environmentally damaging.
choices.explanation: We never hear about any refrigerant chemicals made today, so we have no support to say anything about them.
